To do so, include the ARN of a KMS key in the `kmsKeyArn` field when making a RetrieveAndGenerate request. Attach the following policy, replacing the example values with your own AWS Region, account ID, and AWS KMS key ID to allow Amazon Bedrock to encrypt the session context.\\n\\n#### Using JSON\\n\\n#### Using\\n\\n```\\n{\\n \\\"Version\\\":\\\"2012-10-17\\\",\\n \\\"Statement\\\": [\\n {\\n \\\"Effect\\\": \\\"Allow\\\",\\n \\\"Principal\\\": {\\n \\\"Service\\\": \\\"bedrock.amazonaws.com\\\"\\n },\\n \\\"Action\\\": [\\n \\\"kms:GenerateDataKey\\\",\\n \\\"kms:Decrypt\\\"\\n ],\\n \\\"Resource\\\": \\\"[redacted ARN]\\\"\\n }\\n ]\\n}\\n\\n```\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/encryption-kb.html\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Secure a generative AI assistant with OWASP Top 10 mitigation | Artificial Intelligence\",\"context\":\"## RAG data store layer\\n\\nThe RAG data store is responsible for securely retrieving up-to-date, precise, and user access-controlled knowledge from various first-party and third-party data sources. When setting up a data ingestion job for your knowledge base, you can also encrypt the job using a custom AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key.\\n\\nIf you decide to use the vector store in Amazon OpenSearch Service for your knowledge base, Amazon Bedrock can pass a KMS key of your choice to it for encryption. Additionally, you can encrypt the sessions in which you generate responses from querying a knowledge base with a KMS key. To facilitate secure communication, Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases uses TLS encryption when interacting with third-party vector stores, provided that the service supports and permits TLS encryption in transit.\\n\\nRegarding user access control, Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases uses filters to manage permissions. To keep the access controls updated, you should periodically resync the data to reflect any changes in permissions. Additionally, groups can be stored as a filterable attribute, further refining access control.\\n\\nThis approach helps mitigate the risk of LLM02:2025 Sensitive Information Disclosure and LLM08:2025 Vector & Embedding Weaknesses, to assist in that only authorized users can access the relevant data\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/secure-a-generative-ai-assistant-with-owasp-top-10-mitigation/\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Search docs for Bedrock knowledge base encryption check"}

- `serverSideEncryptionConfiguration.kmsKeyArn` is a real field. It holds the ARN of the KMS key used to encrypt a managed knowledge base's resources.
- When it's absent, Bedrock still encrypts knowledge base data, using an AWS-owned or AWS-managed key by default. A customer-managed key is optional. kb-b is therefore encrypted at rest, just not with a key you control.

**What I can't confirm**
- Whether your tool treats a missing customer-managed key as a finding at all. That is a policy choice in the tool. Some tools flag it, and others treat the default encryption as compliant.
- What severity or finding format the tool uses.
- Whether kb-b yields one finding or several. A missing `serverSideEncryptionConfiguration` could produce one finding, or none, depending on how the check is written.

**My expectation, not something I verified**
- kb-a should pass, or emit nothing, because it has a customer-managed key.
- kb-b would most plausibly produce a single finding at most, for "no customer-managed KMS key configured". That is only a guess about how a typical check would behave.

To get a firm answer, tell me which tool or rule set this is, such as a Security Hub control, an AWS Config rule, Prowler, or an in-house scanner.
